Now let me compile everything I've gathered into a verse-by-verse commentary. I was unable to search some specific traditions (Methodist, Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, modern scholarship, Word of Faith/Hyper-grace) due to search limits, but I will note that below. Here are the notes:

---

## 1 Samuel 12 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

This chapter contains Samuel's farewell address at Gilgal during Saul's official coronation (1 Samuel 11:14–15). It is one of the theological high points of the Former Prophets, comparable to Joshua 24, Judges 2, and 1 Kings 8. Samuel "closes the books" on his role as national leader, passes the baton to Saul, but makes clear that having a king does not free Israel from obedience to the Lord. — Precept Austin ([URL](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-12-commentary)), Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

**The chapter's structure:**
- vv. 1–5: Samuel's integrity affirmed
- vv. 6–12: A history lesson on God's righteous acts
- vv. 13–15: The choice: obey or rebel
- vv. 16–19: The sign of thunder and rain
- vv. 20–25: Counsel, comfort, warning

---

### v. 1 — "I have listened to your voice … I have set over you a king."

Samuel reminds all Israel that the monarchy was *their* idea, not his. He "obeyed their voice" because God had commanded him to do so (1 Samuel 8:7), even though he personally disagreed. Samuel wants it clear that he did not push for a king; he simply carried out God's directive in response to the people's demand. — Enduring Word / Guzik ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/)), Precept Austin ([URL](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-12-commentary))

Ellicott notes this is the "real inauguration of the earthly monarchy" and that many of the very words Samuel spoke were preserved and treasured in Israel's memory. Samuel, the "link between the judges and the kings," presents Saul to the people as "the Anointed of the Eternal." — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

---

### v. 2 — "Now here is the king walking before you, and I am old and gray … my sons are here with you."

Samuel points to Saul standing beside him. "Walking before you" is shepherd imagery — the king is now to lead the flock, going before them as a shepherd does his sheep (cf. John 10:27). — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

"I am old and gray" echoes what the elders had said in 1 Samuel 8:5 — Samuel concedes the point. He mentions "my sons are with you" to show that his sons have been removed from public office and reduced to the level of ordinary citizens, no longer judges. — Ellicott; Guzik notes that this was Samuel's humble submission to having removed his corrupt sons from leadership. — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/)), Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

Precept Austin notes: "Samuel is a perfect example of an OT saint who 'died to self!'" — he willingly relinquished power and did not pass prestige to his sons. — Precept Austin ([URL](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-12-commentary))

---

### v. 3 — "Here I am. Bear witness against me … Whose ox or donkey have I taken? … I will restore it to you."

Samuel's final act as judge was to put *himself* on trial. He is the defendant, the people are prosecutors, and the Lord and His anointed are the enforcing authorities. — Precept Austin ([URL](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-12-commentary))

He challenges the nation on three specific points: theft ("whose ox or donkey"), oppression/fraud, and bribery. Samuel knew his sons had been accused of taking bribes (1 Samuel 8:3); by this challenge he distances himself from their corruption. — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

Guzik notes: Samuel's offer "I will restore it" shows humility — he was open to the possibility he may have wronged someone unknowingly and wanted to make it right. — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

Ellicott observes this is the earliest instance of a king bearing the title "His Anointed" (Messiah/Christ), a title previously used for the high priest but now transferred to the king. — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

---

### v. 4 — "You have not wronged us or oppressed us … nor have you taken anything from the hand of man."

Israel unanimously affirms Samuel's blameless record. He led them not for what he could get, but for what he could give. — Enduring Word / Guzik ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

Grant's Commentary: "Sad it is to say that not many men in authority could stand up to a test of this kind. But Samuel had learned early in life to depend upon the pure grace of God, the result being a steady, consistent life of truth and stability." — Grant's Commentary, StudyLight ([URL](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/1-samuel-12.html))

---

### v. 5 — "The LORD is a witness against you, and His anointed is a witness today … He is a witness."

Samuel calls God and Saul as witnesses to the people's testimony. Guzik notes two reasons: (1) if Israel later accused Samuel of wrong, he could call them back to this day's testimony; (2) if they tried to blame Saul's failures on Samuel, this testimony would be a witness against them. Deliberately including Saul makes the leadership transition crystal clear. — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

Ellicott observes that the Hebrew dramatically picks up the people's cry from v. 4: Samuel says "even the Eternal" — the same God who raised up Moses and Aaron is the witness. — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

---

### v. 6 — "The LORD is the One who appointed Moses and Aaron, and who brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt."

Having cleared his own name, Samuel now turns to "plead with" the people concerning God's righteous acts. He begins with the Exodus — the foundational act of redemption by which the Eternal assumed sovereignty over Israel. — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

Guzik: Samuel focuses not on the history of Israel but on "the history of the righteous acts of the LORD." — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

---

### v. 7 — "Now present yourselves, so that I may confront you before the LORD with all the righteous acts He has done."

Samuel frames what follows as a legal confrontation — a covenant lawsuit. He is placing Israel "in the dock," with witnesses from Israel's past: Moses, Aaron, Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah — all men used by God to deliver His people. — Precept Austin ([URL](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-12-commentary))

Piper: "How do you plead with people concerning the past? You can't change the past; you can only change the future. So what Samuel must mean is: I plead with you to recognize what it implies that God has done these things for you. I urge you to act in the future like people who believe God will take care of them as he did in the past." — Desiring God / Piper ([URL](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-evil-origin-of-a-good-king))

---

### v. 8 — "When Jacob went to Egypt … He sent them Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place."

The first "righteous act": the Exodus and settlement in Canaan. Samuel begins the pattern: God saves → people sin → God disciplines → people repent → God delivers. — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

---

### v. 9 — "But they forgot the LORD their God, and He sold them into the hand of Sisera … the Philistines … the king of Moab."

The second element of the pattern: when Israel forgot God, He "sold them" — a deliberate act of divine chastisement. Guzik emphasizes that Samuel frames even God's discipline as one of His "righteous acts": "His discipline is just as righteous as His deliverance." — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

Ellicott notes the three oppressors named (Canaanites under Sisera, Philistines, Moabites under Eglon) are listed without strict chronological order, as the point is thematic, not sequential. — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

---

### v. 10 — "They cried out to the LORD … 'We have sinned, for we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and Ashtoreths.'"

The third element: repentance. The people confessed specific sins — forsaking the Lord and serving Baal and Ashtaroth (the chief male and female deities of the Canaanites/Phoenicians). Ellicott notes the plural forms "Baalim and Ashtaroth" refer to various local personifications of these deities. — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

---

### v. 11 — "So the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel, and He delivered you."

The fourth element: God's merciful deliverance. "Jerubbaal" is Gideon (Judges 6:32). The BSB reads "Barak" (so the LXX and Syriac), but the Hebrew text reads "Bedan." Ellicott explains the letters for Bedan and Barak are similar in Hebrew and a scribal error may have occurred. Some Jewish commentators (Kimchi) suggest "Bedan" = "Ben-Dan" (son of Dan), i.e., Samson. — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

Guzik notes Samuel includes himself in the list: "No judge had accomplished such great things for the people, and none had received more general recognition." — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

---

### v. 12 — "But when you saw that Nahash king of the Ammonites was moving against you, you said to me, 'No, we must have a king to rule over us' — even though the LORD your God was your king."

Here is the indictment's climax. The people's "No!" was a rejection of God as king. Instead of crying out to the Lord as they had in the past, they demanded a human king. — Desiring God / Piper ([URL](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-evil-origin-of-a-good-king))

Piper underscores: they wanted to be "like all the nations" (1 Samuel 8:5). Their sin was not merely the request but the motive — replacing trust in God with trust in human institutions, seeking worldly similarity rather than spiritual distinctiveness. — Desiring God ([URL](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-evil-origin-of-a-good-king))

Grant: "This was virtually telling God that He was no longer to be trusted as their king!" — Grant's Commentary, StudyLight ([URL](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/1-samuel-12.html))

---

### v. 13 — "Now here is the king you have chosen, the one you requested. Behold, the LORD has placed a king over you."

Two sides of one transaction: the people chose Saul; the Lord *set* him over them. The Pulpit Commentary: "The people had desired a king, chosen and appointed by themselves, to represent the nation in temporal matters; Jehovah gave them a king to represent himself, with authority coming from God, and limited by God." — Pulpit Commentary, StudyLight ([URL](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-12.html))

Guzik: "Samuel probably had the feeling, 'Here is the king you wanted. You will find that he isn't quite the king you need, but he is the king you wanted.'" — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

---

### vv. 14–15 — "If you fear the LORD … then all will be well. But if you disobey … the hand of the LORD will be against you."

The Pulpit Commentary notes that v. 14 is an unfinished sentence in Hebrew: "If ye will fear Jehovah … and if both ye and the king … will follow Jehovah your God, *it shall be well*." Samuel "piles up one upon another the conditions of their happiness, and then from the depth of his emotion breaks off, leaving the blessed consequences of their obedience unsaid." — Pulpit Commentary, StudyLight ([URL](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-12.html))

Ellicott agrees: "The intense wish, 'O that you would only fear the Lord! O that you and your king would only continue following!' is contained in the Hebrew particle." A similar unfinished sentence is found in Luke 19:42. — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

Guzik: "One wrong turn did not put them out of God's plan forever." Even after their sinful demand for a king, God placed before them a clear choice: obedience or rebellion. They are not a special exception; God will deal with them as He dealt with their fathers. — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

---

### vv. 16–17 — "Now, therefore, stand and see this great thing … Is it not the wheat harvest today? I will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain."

Samuel volunteers a sign to confirm his words. The wheat harvest in Canaan falls between mid-May and mid-June — a time when rain is extremely rare. MacLaren asks: why was Samuel so certain God would answer? "Because he recognised that the impulse to proffer the sign came from God … It is when we ask 'anything according to His will' that we know that 'He heareth us.'" — MacLaren, StudyLight ([URL](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/1-samuel-12.html))

Spurgeon preached a famous sermon on this verse (his first ever printed sermon, August 1854), using the harvest as a picture of God's work in the world. — Spurgeon, StudyLight ([URL](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-samuel-12.html))

Guzik notes: thunder and rain during harvest was not merely a power display — heavy rain could destroy crops. The sign carried both power and a warning of judgment. — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

Ellicott: "Rain in that season seldom or never falls, but if it does it is usually severe … coming, as it did, in direct answer to the seer's invocation, struck the people naturally with great fear." — Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm))

---

### v. 18 — "So Samuel called to the LORD, and on that day the LORD sent thunder and rain. As a result, all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel."

The sign demonstrated Samuel's power in prayer. He is known in Scripture as a mighty intercessor (Psalm 99:6, Jeremiah 15:1). Guzik observes that the people's fear was good, but it also revealed something carnal: they should have already known God's power in their hearts rather than needing a sign. — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

---

### v. 19 — "Pray to the LORD your God for your servants so that we will not die! For we have added to all our sins the evil of asking for a king."

At last Israel sees and confesses their sin. Guzik: "They saw it too late; if only they had realized it in 1 Samuel 8, when Samuel first warned them!" Yet now they are stuck with a king — but God could still turn it for good if they repented. — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

Piper presents this as a picture of gospel grace: the people are terrified, confess their spectacular sin, and what follows (v. 20) is free grace to sinners. — Desiring God / Piper ([URL](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-sinful-origin-of-the-son-of-david))

---

### v. 20 — "Do not be afraid … Even though you have committed all this evil, do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart."

Samuel does not minimize their sin — "You have done all this wickedness" — but he refuses to let them drown in guilt. The focus must be on serving God *now*, with all their heart. Guzik: "Satan loves it when we live in the past or in the future, when we do anything but serve the LORD with all we have right now." — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

Piper's third lesson from the chapter: "If the plight in which you find yourself is irreversible and it was your own sin that got you there, do not be paralyzed by guilt and despair." — Desiring God / Piper ([URL](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-evil-origin-of-a-good-king))

---

### v. 21 — "Do not turn aside after worthless things that cannot profit you or deliver you, for they are empty."

Idols are "empty things" (Hebrew *tohu* — the same word used in Genesis 1:2 for the formless void). They cannot profit, deliver, or satisfy. Guzik: "If they would not serve God for spiritual reasons, then let them do it simply to succeed because nothing else can profit or deliver." — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

---

### v. 22 — "Indeed, for the sake of His great name, the LORD will not abandon His people, because He was pleased to make you His own."

This is one of the most theologically rich verses in the chapter. Piper devoted an entire sermon to it ("The Pleasure of God in His Name"). His key point: "The LORD will not forsake his people, *for his great name's sake*." It does not say "for their great name's sake." God's faithfulness is rooted in His allegiance to His own name, not in Israel's worthiness. — Desiring God ([URL](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-evil-origin-of-a-good-king))

The Pulpit Commentary: though v. 14 made Israel's well-being dependent on their conduct, in a higher sense it depended on God's will. He chose Israel not for its own sake (Deuteronomy 7:7–8) but for His redemptive purposes, and so the nation must continue according to God's promises despite severe chastisements. — Pulpit, StudyLight ([URL](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-12.html))

Piper goes further: "God's first love is his name and not his people. And because it is, there is hope for his sinful people." Grace flows to sinners precisely from God's supreme allegiance to His own name. — Desiring God / Piper ([URL](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-sinful-origin-of-the-son-of-david))

---

### v. 23 — "As for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you. And I will continue to teach you the good and right way."

Samuel names two ongoing duties: intercessory prayer and teaching. The Pulpit Commentary notes: "In no character of the Old Testament does this duty of intercessory prayer stand forward so prominently as in Samuel" — and he did not rest content with prayer alone, but added teaching. Samuel also made provision for future teachers by founding the schools of the prophets. — Pulpit, StudyLight ([URL](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-12.html))

Guzik cites Spurgeon: "Samuel had become so rooted in the habit of prayer for the people that he seems to start at the very thought of bringing his intercession to an end." Guzik adds: "It is a sin for a leader of God's people to stop praying for them. It is the most basic of his duties as a leader. If it is a sin to stop praying, how much worse must it be to even fail to start praying!" — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

---

### v. 24 — "Above all, fear the LORD and serve Him faithfully with all your heart; consider what great things He has done for you."

Samuel brings his address to a positive close. All service and obedience are to be responses to what God has *already* done, not attempts to earn His favor. Guzik: "We can only keep perspective in our Christian lives if we keep focused on what great things He has done for us." — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

Piper notes that this verse echoes v. 7 — Samuel pleads the past for the sake of the future. "We know the sort of God we are counting on tomorrow, only because we can see the way he acted yesterday." — Desiring God / Piper ([URL](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-evil-origin-of-a-good-king))

---

### v. 25 — "But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away."

The final warning — and it proved prophetic. Guzik cites Clarke: "Never was a people more fully warned, and never did a people profit less by the warning." This became the sad legacy of Israel through the conquests and exiles. — Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

---

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed / Baptist (Sovereignty Emphasis) — John Piper

Piper's reading (from Desiring God, broadly Reformed Baptist) stresses that the kingship arose through a "spectacular sin," yet God sovereignly planned it. He makes four lessons:

1. **The way we seek something can be wrong even when the thing itself is not wrong.** Having a king was not inherently evil; it was the motive (to be like the nations, to replace God) that made it a great wickedness.
2. **God's sovereign purposes are fulfilled even through the sins of His people.** God predicted the kingship in Deuteronomy 17:14–20 long before; the sin did not take Him by surprise.
3. **If your plight is irreversible and caused by your own sin, do not be paralyzed by guilt.** Acknowledge the sin, then serve the Lord with all your heart (v. 20).
4. **God's faithfulness is rooted in His allegiance to His own name** (v. 22), not in human merit. This is the ground of all hope for sinners.

— Desiring God / Piper ([URL](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-evil-origin-of-a-good-king)), also "The Sinful Origin of the Son of David" ([URL](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-sinful-origin-of-the-son-of-david))

### Pentecostal / Charismatic — David Guzik (Enduring Word)

Guzik's approach (Enduring Word is broadly evangelical with charismatic sympathies) emphasizes:
- The power of prayer: Samuel is "a mighty man of prayer," and his prayer life is held up as the model for all believers — not just leaders. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "Perhaps you will never preach, but you may pray. If you cannot climb the pulpit you may bow before the mercy-seat, and be quite as great a blessing."
- The miraculous sign: God confirms His word with supernatural intervention in nature. Samuel knew God would answer because he was in tune with God's will.
- Spiritual warfare: Satan loves to distract believers into living in past regret or future worry rather than serving God with all their heart *now* (v. 20).

— Enduring Word ([URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-12/))

### Older / Classic Evangelical — Pulpit, Ellicott, MacLaren

These older commentaries stress:
- The pathos of Samuel's farewell and the "unfinished sentence" of v. 14 as evidence of deep emotion.
- Samuel as a type of Christ — the faithful prophet who intercedes and teaches.
- The two-sided nature of the monarchy: both human choice and divine appointment (v. 13).

— Pulpit Commentary (StudyLight), Ellicott ([URL](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/12.htm)), MacLaren (StudyLight)

---
